title: The structure of the Arabic name

blocks.text: A complete Arabic name may contain a lot of information: the proper name, the name of the father and grandfather, a nickname, an origin, sometimes the name of a son. Who reads documents, lists or news must be able to break down a name and understand which part is from "name" and which from "name" because they do not always correspond to the boxes of European forms. This unit opens the trace of onomastics (ONO-01 and ONO-02): here you study the parts of the name and their order; in ONO-02 Latin graphs and variants. A week.

Targets. At the end of the lesson you know:
1. recognize the five traditional parts of the name: ism, nasab, kunya, laqab, nisba;
2. read and write ⁧ابن⁩ / ⁧بن⁩ / ⁧بنت⁩ and distinguish ⁧آل⁩ The family of the person (s) from Article ⁧الـ⁩ ;
3. recognizing composite names ( ⁧عَبْد الله⁩ , ⁧نُور الدِّين⁩ ) and do not break them;
4. understand how a name appears on documents in different areas of the Arab world;
5. I'll introduce you under the full name and ask someone for his full name.

Note of method. A name says something about the traditions of names, not about a person's identity. A Nisba as ⁧المِصْرِيّ⁩ "Egyptian" may be a surname inherited from generations; a name "religious" does not say what the bearer believes; many names pass from one country to another. From a name you never deduce nationality, religion or origin: you read the data of the document and ask the person. Texts. From this unit the texts are partially vocized: vowels on new words, forms in study and where reading is ambiguous; desinences only where they serve. Tables and examples remain vocalized. In the classic name the parts can appear all, in a fairly fixed order: kunya + ism + nasab + nisba (the laqab can be at the beginning or at the end). In the modern name, the parts have changed: the nasab became the chain + father's name + grandpa's name, and many laqab and nisba have become family surnames (section 7).
